texts.full_text: s a dare—a challenge to the audience's courage and willingness to confront an unvarnished, brutal reality that many of us prefer to ignore or deny in our quest for entertainment. The film follows Henry Fonda (Michael Moriarty), who is introduced working at a butcher shop. His job involves cleaning up after autopsies—a task he performs with the same meticulous care and precision as if it were his own personal art form, which sets an unsettling tone from early on. Henry's life takes a dark turn when he becomes obsessed with murdering people for fun; this obsession is fueled by his fascination with death and decay. The film delves into the psyche of Henry Fonda in gruesome detail—showcasing how his mind works, what drives him to commit these horrific acts. The cinematography captures a gritty realism that adds an extra layer of discomfort for viewers; it's as if we're being invited inside Henry’s twisted world. The film is not just about the violence itself but also delves into themes such as loneliness and isolation, which are central to understanding why someone might turn towards such extreme behaviors. The performances by Michael Moriarty in particular stand out—he manages to portray a deeply disturbed individual without descending into caricature or cliché. The supporting cast is equally strong; they bring depth and complexity that elevate the film beyond mere shock value, making it an exploration of human nature at its darkest. Henry: Portrait of a Serial Killer (1986) may not be for everyone—it's certainly not something I would recommend to casual viewers or those who are easily disturbed. But I was surprised when I stumbled upon the following Rust code: Option<Option<i32>> We know that Rust has a >> shift operator, so I think a naive tokenizer would output a >> token here, which the parser would see as an error (because it expects two > tokens instead). But clearly the Rust compiler understands the situation and handles it correctly. What's going on here? Does the tokenizer keep some state, somehow knowing that it needs to close an angle bracket? Does the parser check for >> and break it into two tokens that are pushed back into 2 > tokens if they're not followed by = in this context? Or is there something else going on. 1 Answer active oldest votes up vote 9 down vote accepted The tokenizers job stops at separating raw code input into smaller units. A lexer may have a buffer of characters it hasn't yet produced, because for example two subsequent > can either >> or < followed by an pattern like Option<>. Therefore the decision is deferred until a complete expression has been found and we are certain that this could not be a shift operator. share | improve this answer answered May 6 at 17:02 blaffie 21.2k

Overview TheNorthern Saw-whet Owl (Aegolius acadius) is a small but mighty owl species found across North America. Named for its distinctive saw-like "saw whet" call and unique ear tufts resembling the ears of a mouse, this bird has captivated both scientists and enthusiasts alike. ID Info - Size: 7"-9" - Wingspan: about 18 inches - Plumage coloration varies from brown to gray-brown with distinctive white "spots" or streaks on its back. - Has prominent ear tufts, yellow eyes surrounded by black feathers (giving the appearance of a mask), and no visible neck. Life History Northern Saw-whet Owls are nocturnal creatures that prefer mature forests for nesting.
